items.text: Pip has too many beads to count one by one!
Ten ones can click together into one ten.
Make as many tens as you can.
Then count tens and the ones left over.
Can you make one more ten from the ones?
Ten lanterns stack into one tower!
Make as many hundreds as you can from the tens.
Can you make a hundred from 10 of the tens?
Pip found some beads in the meadow. How many are there?
Count the hundreds, then the tens, then the ones.
Start with the big squares. How many hundreds?
Each square is 100, each rod is 10, each cube is 1.
Every digit lives in a house: hundreds, tens or ones.
In 372, the 3 is in the hundreds house, so it is worth 300.
The 7 is in the tens house, so it is worth 70.
The 2 is in the ones house, so it is worth 2.
Which house is that digit in?
A digit in the tens house is worth that many tens.
A number can be split into its places.
Each part is one place: hundreds, tens, ones.
Put the parts back together to make the number.
Hundreds, tens and ones each get their own place.
Pip hears a number name. Can you write it?
"Four hundred six" means 4 hundreds and 6 ones.
There are no tens, so the tens place holds a 0.
How many hundreds? How many tens? How many ones?
Write one digit for each place, using 0 for an empty place.
Pip hops along the number path.
Counting by 10s changes the tens digit.
Counting by 100s changes the hundreds digit.
Counting by 5s goes 0, 5, 0, 5 in the ones.
How much does each jump add?
Add the same jump each time.
Some houses are empty. Zero keeps their spot.
4 hundreds and 5 ones has no tens.
Write a 0 in the tens place: 405.
Zero holds a place so the other digits stay put.
A hundred is also ten tens.
Each hundred is 10 tens, so 3 hundreds is 30 tens.
How many tens are in the hundreds?
Count all the tens, including the ones inside the hundreds.
Two ferries are racing. Which one carries more?
If the hundreds are the same, compare the tens.
If the tens are the same too, compare the ones.
The number with more hundreds is bigger, no matter what the tens and ones say.
Where does this number live on the line?
Find how much each jump is.
Count the jumps to the arrow.
Pip adds one more lantern, or one more tower. What changes?
Adding 10 adds one ten. Only the tens digit changes.
Adding 100 adds one hundred. Only the hundreds digit changes.
Which place gets one more, or one less?
10 more means one more ten. Keep the ones the same.
Find the two tens the number sits between.
5 or more goes up; 4 or less goes down.
Which two tens is it between?
The ones digit decides: 5 or more rounds up.
Find the two hundreds the number sits between.
Which two hundreds is it between?
The tens digit decides when rounding to the nearest 100.
To add, count on from the bigger number.
To subtract, count back, or think of the adding fact.
Start from the bigger number and count on.
Start counting on the next number.
Make a ten to add faster!
8 + 5: give 2 from the 5 to the 8 to make 10.
How many more does the first number need to make 10?
Fill the ten-frame first, then add what is left.
Adding and subtracting are a family.
If you know one fact, you know the family.
What adding fact uses these numbers?
The ferry carries two groups of beads across the river.
Add the ones to the ones.
Add the tens to the tens.
Ones add with ones, tens add with tens.
Too many ones for one dock! Ten ones can ride together as one ten.
Add the ones. If you get 10 or more, make a ten.
Move the new ten to the tens place.
Add the tens, including the new one.
Look at the ones. Is it more than 9?
Ten ones make one ten. Carry it to the tens.
Some beads hop off the ferry. How many stay?
Take the ones from the ones.
Take the tens from the tens.
Ones from ones, tens from tens.
Not enough ones to take away? Break a ten into ten ones.
Look at the ones. Can you take the bottom ones from the top ones?
If not, break one ten into ten ones.
Now there is one fewer ten. Subtract each place.
Can you take those ones away? If not, break a ten.
Break one ten into ten ones, then remember there is one less ten.
The ferry carries three or four groups at once!
Add all the tens, including the new ones.
Ones first, make tens, then add the tens.
Can you make one number a ten?
Move a little from one number to the other to make a ten.
How far is it from one number to the other?
Hop to the next ten first.
A big ferry with hundreds, tens and ones!
Add the ones, and make a ten if you need to.
Add the tens, and make a hundred if you need to.
Start with the ones. Did you get 10 or more?
Ten tens make one hundred, just like ten ones make one ten.
Break a ten, or break a hundred, when there are not enough.
Start with the ones. Break a ten if you need to.
Then the tens. Break a hundred if you need to.
Start with the ones. Is the top digit big enough?
Break one of the next place when a place is too small.
Not enough tens either? Break a hundred.
Break a hundred into 10 tens, then a ten into 10 ones.
There are no tens to break. What can you break instead?
Break a hundred into tens, then a ten into ones.
Add ones, then tens, then hundreds.
Carry when a place makes 10 or more.
Line up places, add right to left, carry tens.
Break a ten or a hundred when a place is too small.
Is the top digit big enough?
Line up places, subtract right to left, regroup when needed.
Round each number to the nearest hundred.
Use it to check if an exact answer makes sense.
Rounded numbers give a quick check.
Ten ones are the same as one ten.
That is why we carry a ten, or break one.
Think about what ten ones are worth.
Every carry and every break is a trade of 10 for 1.
If none is left over, the number is even.
If one is left over, it is odd.
Make pairs. Is one left over?
Even numbers split into pairs with none left.
Add the same number for each row.
How many in each row? How many rows?
Add the row amount once for each row.
Pip plants seeds in equal rows in the orchard.
Equal groups is what times means.
How many groups? How many in each?
Add the same number again for each group.
Hop along by the same amount.
Skip-count by the number in each group.
Where you land is the product.
How many hops? How big is each hop?
Turn the array on its side: 6 rows of 3.
Does turning the array change the number of dots?
Swapping the numbers does not change the product.
Count by 2s, 5s and 10s to multiply fast.
× 5: count by fives, or half of × 10.
× 10: put a zero on the end, because each one becomes a ten.
Times 10 makes each one a ten. Times 5 is half of that.
Anything times 0 is 0: groups with nothing inside.
Anything times 1 is itself: one group.
How many are in each group?
What is the × 2 fact? Now double it.
Double to go from 2s to 4s, and 4s to 8s.
The nines trick: ten groups take away one.
What is 10 groups? Now take one group away.
9 groups is 10 groups minus one group.
Use two facts you know and add them.
Use a fact you know nearby.
Which fact nearby do you know?
Start from a known fact and add or take away a group.
How many groups of that number make the total?
How many tens is that number?
Multiply the tens, then name them as tens.
Times an even number is even.
Look for a pattern you know.
Odd × odd is odd; anything × even is even.
Use your strategies to work out any fact.
Every fact can be built from one you know.
Draw the story as a bar.
Is the start, the change or the end missing?
Add or subtract to find it.
Draw the story. What is missing?
Find the missing part of the story, then choose the operation.
Split it into the two parts.
If a part is missing, subtract. If the whole is missing, add.
Is a part missing, or the whole?
Who has more, and how many more?
The difference is the extra piece.
Draw two bars. How long is the extra piece?
"How many more" means find the difference.
Use the first answer in the second step.
What happens first in the story?
Do step one, then use its answer for step two.
Pip's puzzle: find 100 − 37 without breaking a ten!
Take every digit from 9, except the last one.
It works because 100 is 99 + 1, and 99 never needs regrouping.
All from 9, and the last from 10.
100 is 99 + 1. Subtract from the 9s, then add the 1 to the last place.

This trick appears in the 1965 book Vedic Mathematics by Bharati Krishna Tirtha. Historians note it is not found in the ancient Vedas themselves. We teach it because the math is sound and it is useful.
